en.title: Nice to Monaco
en.excerpt: Sea views, a mostly flat start on Nice’s promenade, coastal climbs and a poolside finish in Monaco.
en.body:
In mid-May 2023, I ran from near Nice airport to Monaco. The GPX route below covers about 25.3 km one way, with roughly 230 m of accumulated climbing. From the promenade in Nice all the way to Monaco, the views were excellent. There were climbs and a few sections where I needed to pay attention to the road, but nothing I found impossible compared to some other places. The run ended with a sun lounger beside a proper outdoor pool in Monaco. The weather was on my side too. 

## Start: the Nice promenade

I started near the airport and made my way along Nice's promenade. This was the most straightforward part of the run, and it felt very flat and safe. The sea was right there - easy place to settle into the run.

## Hills, roadside sections and a useful drink stop

Once I was away from the promenade, the route became more varied. There were climbs, but they were manageable. Some sections ran beside the road between the hills, so I had to be more careful there than on the promenade. I also ran past Cap Roux, another beautiful spot on this stretch of the coast.  There was also a petrol station around halfway to Monaco, where I could buy a quick drink and use bathroom. French riviera is a beautiful thing and most of the time during the run, I was just enjoying the views.

## The coastal path into Monaco

On the approach to Monaco, I followed the beautiful [Cap-d’Ail coastal path](https://www.explorenicecotedazur.com/nature/sentier-du-littoral-de-cap-dail/), with the sea beside me and the path running between the rocks. It was a lovely way to arrive after the road sections and the hills.

![The rocky coastal path at Cap-d'Ail beside the Mediterranean](/assets/uploads/nice-to-monaco/cap-dail-coastal-path.jpg "The coastal path at Cap-d'Ail.")

Photo: [Renek78 / Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Littoral_path_between_Plage_de_la_Mala_and_Plage_Marquet_in_Cap-d%27Ail_01.jpg), [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/).

## Monaco*: a poolside finish

Monaco* is included in this France story because this was one coastal run from Nice, and the beautiful cliffside path on the approach is actually at Cap-d’Ail, in France. Monaco itself is small, with narrow streets, limited space and plenty of tourists, so I found it awkward for uninterrupted running. That does not make it a bad place: I loved the finish here, and the coastal stretch towards Monaco ranks in my personal top three. The score below reflects that run, rather than running around central Monaco.

Preparations for the Formula 1 race were underway when I arrived. The main start-finish straight was closed to traffic, so I took the opportunity to run along it before heading to the pool.

On my 2023 visit, €12 covered a shower and a day on a sun lounger beside the pool. A friend who visited a few months ago in 2026 reported the same price. The large, well-kept pool made for an excellent finish, and I noticed several people with Ironman backpacks there for swim training. Check the [municipality’s pool information](https://mairie.mc/le-stade-nautique-rainier-iii) for a future visit.

There was time for an ice cream too:

![Me eating an ice cream in Monaco, with Grand Prix preparations behind me](/assets/uploads/nice-to-monaco/monaco-ice-cream.jpg "An ice cream in Monaco after the run, with F1 preparations in the background.")

## Where the route is flat and where it climbs

The easiest opening follows the Promenade des Anglais and Quai des États-Unis towards Port Lympia, Nice’s harbour. For roughly the first 6 km, the supplied GPX stays mostly around 7 to 14 m above sea level. This is the part I would choose for relaxed, continuous coastal kilometres.

Leaving Port Lympia is where it starts to feel hillier. Around 7 to 8 km, the route climbs onto Boulevard Carnot, towards the Cap de Nice side of the coast. It rises from roughly 15 m to around 65 m, so this is the first clear change from the flatter promenade.

There is another climb through Villefranche-sur-Mer, around 11 to 12 km, on the Avenue Albert 1er section. The profile reaches about 76 m before descending towards Beaulieu-sur-Mer, getting close to sea level again around 14 km. That descent is a useful breather after the earlier climbs.

The stretch through Beaulieu-sur-Mer towards Èze-Bord-de-Mer, approximately 14 to 18 km, is gentler, although there is still a small rise. The longer later climb begins around the Èze-Bord-de-Mer coastal area, then continues towards Cap-d’Ail along the Basse Corniche, roughly 18 to 21 km into this route. This is the coastal side below Èze village, rather than a climb up to the hilltop village. The GPX builds from around 20 m to its highest point of about 93 m here, so I would allow more effort and time for this part.

Cap-d’Ail brings the relief of heading back down towards the coast. By about 22 to 23 km, the route is near sea level again. The coastal approach towards Monaco, around 23 to 24 km, is comparatively flat, before a final short rise in the built-up area near the end. Flatter terrain does not always mean easier running here: narrow paths, roadside sections and people still need attention.

![Elevation profile of the Nice to Monaco route, with a flat opening and several later climbs](/assets/uploads/nice-to-monaco/elevation-profile.svg "About 25.3 km one way and approximately 230 m of climbing, estimated from the supplied GPX. Distances refer to this route; elevations are metres above sea level.")

The profile gives me a useful way to split the run: Nice for the easiest continuous kilometres, the middle and later road sections for the climbing, and the rocky coastal approach for the scenery. None of the climbs felt impossible to me, but this was a more varied outing than a flat promenade run.

## Would I do it again?

For the views, yes. I would keep the same distinction in mind: Nice's promenade felt very easy, while the roadside stretches between the hills needed more attention. The climbs were manageable, and the scenery made the effort worthwhile. This was a run where the surroundings were a big part of the point itself.
## Free run clubs in Nice and Monaco

I have not joined these clubs myself. They are options to explore if you would rather run with a group; check the latest schedule and meeting point before going.

### Nice: Nice Runners

A free, no-registration social group with different distance options and runners of different levels. Their published schedule is Monday, Wednesday and Friday evenings, meeting at Ma Nolan’s on Cours Saleya before heading out along the seafront.

[Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/nicerunners_/) · [Schedule and free-run information](https://www.monaco-tribune.com/en/2025/08/running-on-the-cote-dazur-clubs-and-routes-for-all-levels/)

### Nice: Triathlon Store Run Session

The shop advertises a free, coach-led Saturday run, meeting at 10:20 for a 10:30 departure, outside Triathlon Store, 2 rue Saint-Philippe. Their suggested level is being able to run faster than 10 km/h, so check with the shop about the current outing and pace before joining.

[Shop’s run-session information](https://triathlonstore.fr/pages/run-session)

### Monaco: Monaco Run Club

A free social club with several pace groups, including a run-walk option, and a relaxed atmosphere. Its published programme is Wednesday and Sunday evenings, with meeting points and routes varying around Monaco, so check the club’s latest Instagram or Strava announcement for your session.

[Club report and practical information](https://www.monaco-tribune.com/en/2025/10/we-tried-to-keep-up-with-the-monaco-run-club/) · [Interview with the founders](https://www.montecarlotimes.eu/2025/08/21/monaco-on-the-move-inside-the-energy-of-monaco-run-club/)

Know a club I should add, or spotted something that should be changed or removed? Send me a message on [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/markuskaljuste/) or [Strava](https://strava.app.link/W1a7SCITG7b), and help me keep this useful.
